name: Banaba (Lagerstroemia speciosa)
short: Letter (title only): corosolic acid, a banaba constituent, blamed for kidney injury and lactic acidosis in a patient with poor kidney function; product not named. Reviews: minor or no adverse effects.
text: Safety evidence on banaba is thin. A case letter, which has no abstract, is titled as a report of acute kidney injury and lactic acidosis induced by corosolic acid in a patient with impaired kidney function; the record does not name the product the patient took. Corosolic acid is one of the constituents of banaba, and a 2012 review notes that studies have used water-soluble banaba leaf extracts, extracts standardised to corosolic acid and purified corosolic acid; the title does not say whether the patient took banaba or another product containing corosolic acid. An overview of systematic reviews of herbal medicines listed Lagerstroemia speciosa (banaba) among the herbs with only minor adverse effects; the abstract does not say what those effects were. The same 2012 review stated that no adverse effects had been observed or reported in animal studies or controlled human clinical trials of banaba and corosolic acid. In a 60-day pilot study in 30 people, without a concurrent placebo group, of a tablet combining extracts of banaba leaf, green coffee bean and Moringa oleifera leaf with vitamin D3, no adverse effects were observed and no blood chemistry measurement changed; the findings cannot be attributed to banaba alone. In rats, acute and sub-acute oral toxicity studies of banaba found no deaths or illness and no significant changes in organ weights, blood tests or liver tissue. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
